name: pg-admin-mcp

tools.name: postgres_connection_status
tools.description: Reports resolved configuration, reachability, server version, current-role privileges and the pg_dump/pg_restore/psql client binary versions (which postgres_backup and postgres_restore need) for one named profile or every configured profile (when `profile` is omitted). A profile that fails to load or connect is reported with its error and hint, never thrown — the other profiles still report normally. Never returns a password.

profile.description: Connection profile alias to report on. Omit to report on every configured profile.

tools.name: postgres_list_objects
tools.description: Paginated listing of schemas, tables, views, materialized views, sequences, functions, enum types, and extensions in scope for a profile — the entry point for discovering what exists before describing or querying it. Filter by schema(s), kind(s), and a name pattern. Always returns a nextCursor when more objects remain; pass it back verbatim as cursor to continue. The "enum" kind lists enum types only — domain and composite types are not covered by any kind here.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

schemas.description: Restrict to these schemas. Omit for every schema in scope (Profile.schemas, or every non-system schema).

kinds.description: Restrict to these object kinds (table, partitioned_table, view, materialized_view, foreign_table, schema, sequence, function, enum, extension). Omit for every kind.

namePattern.description: SQL LIKE pattern (% and _ wildcards, \ escapes a literal % or _), matched case-insensitively against the object name via ILIKE.

pageSize.description: Objects per page (max 2000). Defaults to 200, further capped by the profile row limit.

cursor.description: Opaque pagination cursor — pass back the previous call's nextCursor verbatim to fetch the next page.

tools.name: postgres_describe_object
tools.description: Full detail for one object. For a table/partitioned table: columns, primary key, foreign keys in both directions (outbound and what references it), unique/check constraints, indexes (with partial-index predicates), triggers, row-level security, permissions, and comments. A view/materialized view returns its definition; a sequence its parameters and current value; a function its signature and body (all overloads); an enum its labels. An unknown object returns IDENTIFIER_UNKNOWN with near-miss suggestions.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

name.description: Object name within the schema — a table, view, materialized view, sequence, function, or enum type.

tools.name: postgres_get_schema
tools.description: Structured snapshot of a database, or a filtered scope (schemas, kinds, name pattern), composed from the same catalog listings postgres_list_objects uses. detail:"summary" (default) returns names and kinds only — cheap enough for a large database. detail:"full" adds columns, primary key, outbound foreign keys, and indexes for tables/views/materialized views. An oversized result is truncated with an explicit count and a hint for narrowing scope, never silently cut. The "enum" kind lists enum types only — domain and composite types are not covered by any kind here.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

schemas.description: Restrict to these schemas. Omit for every schema in scope (Profile.schemas, or every non-system schema).

kinds.description: Restrict to these object kinds (table, partitioned_table, view, materialized_view, foreign_table, schema, sequence, function, enum, extension). Omit for every kind.

namePattern.description: SQL LIKE pattern (% and _ wildcards, \ escapes a literal % or _), matched case-insensitively against the object name via ILIKE.

detail.description: summary (default): name and kind only — cheap, start here on an unknown or large database. full: adds columns, primary key, outbound foreign keys, and indexes for tables/views/materialized views.

maxObjects.description: Caps the number of objects included before truncation. Defaults to the profile row limit.

tools.name: postgres_select
tools.description: Structured, parameterized, paginated read of one table or view — the primary way to fetch actual row data. Filter with a structured `where` (=, !=, <, <=, >, >=, LIKE, ILIKE, IN, NOT IN, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL); sort with `orderBy` (direction and NULLS FIRST/LAST); page with `limit`/`cursor`. Every identifier is validated against the table's real columns (unknown column -> IDENTIFIER_UNKNOWN with suggestions); every value is a bound parameter. Runs inside a read-only transaction. Not an arbitrary-SQL tool.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

columns.description: Columns to select, in this order. Omit for every column, in ordinal order.

where.description: Filter predicates, ANDed together. Every value is a bound parameter — never interpolated into SQL text.

orderBy.description: Sort columns in priority order. A unique tiebreaker (primary key, or ctid) is appended automatically.

nulls.description: Defaults to the direction's own PostgreSQL default (ASC -> LAST, DESC -> FIRST).

limit.description: Rows per page (max 2000), further capped by the profile row limit.

cursor.description: Opaque pagination cursor — pass back the previous call's nextCursor verbatim to fetch the next page.

tools.name: postgres_explain
tools.description: EXPLAIN a statement (any SQL — SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/etc.) with format (TEXT/JSON/XML/YAML) and flag (costs, buffers, verbose, settings) options. analyze:true actually executes the statement to get real timings — requires the profile's explainAnalyze capability, and is rolled back unless confirm:true is also passed. Without analyze, nothing is ever executed.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

statement.description: The SQL statement to explain — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, etc. Exactly one statement.

analyze.description: EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes statement. Requires the profile's explainAnalyze capability.

format.description: Plan output format. Defaults to TEXT.

confirm.description: Only meaningful with analyze:true. Without it the transaction is always rolled back (dry run) even though ANALYZE really executed statement. With it, the transaction commits normally.

tools.name: postgres_execute_sql
tools.description: The arbitrary-SQL escape hatch — for anything postgres_select cannot express (joins, CTEs, window functions, set operations, catalog queries). Values belong in params ($1, $2, …), which are always bound, never interpolated. Multi-statement strings are refused unless allowMultiple is set, and are impossible when params are supplied. READS run inside a PostgreSQL READ ONLY transaction and return up to `limit` rows; this tool hands out no cursor, so put LIMIT/OFFSET (with an ORDER BY) in your own SQL to read past the cap. WRITES: a statement whose leading keyword is INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE takes the guarded write path when the profile sets PG_<ALIAS>_ALLOW_WRITE=true; UPDATE and DELETE must carry a WHERE clause that references a real column. CREATE/ALTER/DROP/TRUNCATE, COMMENT ON, SECURITY LABEL, REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, CALL and DO additionally need PG_<ALIAS>_ALLOW_DDL=true, and GRANT/REVOKE need PG_<ALIAS>_ALLOW_ADMIN=true. A DDL DRY RUN CANNOT REPORT A ROW COUNT — PostgreSQL returns none for DDL, so a dry-run "0 rows" on a DROP TABLE means "not applicable", never "nothing will happen"; the dry run proves only that the statement parses, resolves and is permitted, and says nothing about how many rows it destroys or what depends on the object. allowMultiple is refused on the write path. No rows are returned by a write, and raw SQL has no catalog-resolved primary key, so there is no key preview and no keyChecksum — which means a production profile refuses raw-SQL writes outright (use postgres_update_batch / postgres_delete_batch / postgres_insert_batch there). A write that no keyword check can see (WITH … INSERT … RETURNING, nextval()) still runs read-only and is still refused by the server; rewrite it as a plain INSERT. Two calls. Call it once WITHOUT confirm to get a dry run: the real mutation runs inside a transaction that is always rolled back, and you get back the true row count, up to 20 affected primary keys, and an `expect` token. Read the row count — it is the guard that matters. Then call again with confirm:true and `expect` passed back verbatim; the server recomputes the hash from your arguments (nothing is stored between calls), re-verifies the row count and key checksum INSIDE the committing transaction, and rolls back instead of committing if anything moved. LIMITATION: keyChecksum is md5 over the sorted primary keys of the affected rows, so it detects a different SET of rows (including a substitution that keeps the count identical) but NOT a change to a row's contents when its primary key and the total row count both stayed the same. envClass=production requires `expect` including keyChecksum and forces allowRowDrift to 0 — the one exception is INSERT, which creates the rows it affects instead of selecting pre-existing ones, so there production verifies the row count alone (still with `expect` and the hash). development accepts a bare confirm:true.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

sql.description: The SQL to run. One statement unless allowMultiple is set. Never string-interpolate values into this — use params.

params.description: Bound parameters for $1, $2, … — always sent over the extended query protocol, so a value is data, never SQL.

allowMultiple.description: Permit several ;-separated statements. Refused by default; impossible together with params.

limit.description: Rows fetched (max 2000), further capped by the profile row limit. Bounds the fetch, not just the response — put LIMIT/OFFSET in your own SQL to read past it.

timeoutMs.description: Per-call statement timeout. Can only tighten the profile's PG_<ALIAS>_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS, never loosen it.

confirm.description: false/omitted (default) = dry run. true = commit, using the `expect` token from the prior dry run.

expect.description: The `expect` token returned by the prior dry run — pass it back verbatim. Required to confirm on staging/production profiles.

allowRowDrift.description: Row-count tolerance between the dry run and the confirm. Forced to 0 on production profiles.

tools.name: postgres_export
tools.description: Streams a table selection or a SELECT statement to a CSV/JSON/JSONL file on disk. Never buffers the full result in memory (a server-side cursor feeds the file in batches), and the file itself is never truncated by the row/byte caps that bound an ordinary tool response. Refuses to overwrite an existing file unless overwrite:true. path resolves against the profile's allowed directories (see postgres_connection_status).

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

columns.description: Columns to export, in this order. Omit for every column, in ordinal order.

where.description: Filter predicates, ANDed together — same shape as postgres_select.

sql.description: A single SELECT (or other row-returning) statement. Never string-interpolate values — use params.

source.description: A structured table+where selection, or a raw SQL source.

path.description: Destination file path. Relative paths resolve against the profile's first allowed directory; absolute paths must still land inside an allowed directory.

overwrite.description: Required (true) to replace an existing file at path. Defaults to false.

timeoutMs.description: Per-call statement timeout — may raise the profile's default, clamped to PG_<ALIAS>_EXPORT_TIMEOUT_MAX_MS.

nullValue.description: Text written for SQL NULL, always unquoted — defaults to "". An actual empty string, and a real value whose text equals this sentinel, are both written quoted so none of the three collide.

tools.name: postgres_copy
tools.description: High-throughput whole-table (or column-subset) transfer through PostgreSQL's own COPY protocol, streamed straight to or from a file — no where filter, no raw SQL source (see postgres_export for those). path resolves against the profile's allowed directories. direction:"export" (default) writes COPY … TO STDOUT to the file. direction:"import" reads the file into the table with COPY … FROM STDIN: it needs PG_<ALIAS>_ALLOW_WRITE=true, refuses a source file larger than PG_MCP_MAX_IMPORT_BYTES (default 512 MiB) before opening it, and goes through the dry-run/confirm protocol below. Two things are specific to import: the row count is COPY's own command tag, and `expect.keyChecksum` is the SHA-256 of the INPUT FILE rather than of affected primary keys (COPY has no RETURNING) — so a key-checksum mismatch on the confirming call means the file changed between the two calls. The file is streamed once for the dry run and once for the confirm. COPY appends rows; it never replaces them. Two calls. Call it once WITHOUT confirm to get a dry run: the real mutation runs inside a transaction that is always rolled back, and you get back the true row count, up to 20 affected primary keys, and an `expect` token. Read the row count — it is the guard that matters. Then call again with confirm:true and `expect` passed back verbatim; the server recomputes the hash from your arguments (nothing is stored between calls), re-verifies the row count and key checksum INSIDE the committing transaction, and rolls back instead of committing if anything moved. LIMITATION: keyChecksum is md5 over the sorted primary keys of the affected rows, so it detects a different SET of rows (including a substitution that keeps the count identical) but NOT a change to a row's contents when its primary key and the total row count both stayed the same. envClass=production requires `expect` including keyChecksum and forces allowRowDrift to 0 — the one exception is INSERT, which creates the rows it affects instead of selecting pre-existing ones, so there production verifies the row count alone (still with `expect` and the hash). development accepts a bare confirm:true.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

direction.description: export (default) = table -> file via COPY … TO STDOUT. import = file -> table via COPY … FROM STDIN, which needs PG_<ALIAS>_ALLOW_WRITE and the confirm protocol below.

columns.description: Columns to copy, in this order. Omit for every column, in ordinal order.

path.description: File path — destination when exporting, source when importing. Relative paths resolve against the profile's first allowed directory; absolute paths must still land inside an allowed directory.

format.description: PostgreSQL COPY format — defaults to csv.

overwrite.description: Export only: required (true) to replace an existing file at path. Defaults to false.

timeoutMs.description: Per-call statement timeout, bounding the whole COPY — may raise the profile's default, clamped to PG_<ALIAS>_EXPORT_TIMEOUT_MAX_MS.

csv.description: Only applies when format is csv (the default) — passed straight through to PostgreSQL's own COPY … WITH options. When importing, these must describe the file you are reading.

confirm.description: false/omitted (default) = dry run. true = commit, using the `expect` token from the prior dry run.

expect.description: The `expect` token returned by the prior dry run — pass it back verbatim. Required to confirm on staging/production profiles.

allowRowDrift.description: Row-count tolerance between the dry run and the confirm. Forced to 0 on production profiles.

tools.name: postgres_insert_batch
tools.description: Bulk INSERT — set-based for ordinary volumes, switching internally to a single-parameter bulk strategy above PG_MCP_INSERT_BULK_THRESHOLD rows (default 1000) to avoid per-column array-serialization overhead on very large batches; both strategies produce identical rows and go through the same guard. Column casts come from the table's real catalog types, never guessed. `onConflict` opts into DO NOTHING or DO UPDATE SET ... FROM EXCLUDED (omitted = plain INSERT, errors on any conflict). There is no WHERE to guard, but every call still goes through the capability check and the dry-run/confirm protocol below. If the table's primary key is server-generated (IDENTITY/SERIAL/DEFAULT nextval) and its column is omitted from `columns`, the confirm step is verified by row count only, not by key checksum — a rolled-back dry run still advances the sequence, so the confirm's real keys would never match a previewed checksum. That holds on production too: an INSERT's affected rows are the rows in your own parameters, which the hash already pins, so this is the one tool a production profile may confirm on row count alone (expect and the hash stay mandatory). Include the key column with an explicit value in `columns`/`rows` if you want checksum-pinned confirmation anyway. Two calls. Call it once WITHOUT confirm to get a dry run: the real mutation runs inside a transaction that is always rolled back, and you get back the true row count, up to 20 affected primary keys, and an `expect` token. Read the row count — it is the guard that matters. Then call again with confirm:true and `expect` passed back verbatim; the server recomputes the hash from your arguments (nothing is stored between calls), re-verifies the row count and key checksum INSIDE the committing transaction, and rolls back instead of committing if anything moved. LIMITATION: keyChecksum is md5 over the sorted primary keys of the affected rows, so it detects a different SET of rows (including a substitution that keeps the count identical) but NOT a change to a row's contents when its primary key and the total row count both stayed the same. envClass=production requires `expect` including keyChecksum and forces allowRowDrift to 0 — the one exception is INSERT, which creates the rows it affects instead of selecting pre-existing ones, so there production verifies the row count alone (still with `expect` and the hash). development accepts a bare confirm:true.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

columns.description: Column names, in the order every row supplies values.

rows.description: Rows to insert, each keyed by column name. A row missing one of "columns" binds NULL for it. Max 20000 rows per call.

target.description: Conflict target columns — must match a unique or exclusion constraint. Required by PostgreSQL when action is "update".

update.description: Columns to overwrite from EXCLUDED on conflict.

onConflict.description: Opt-in ON CONFLICT clause. Omit for a plain INSERT that errors on any conflict.

confirm.description: false/omitted (default) = dry run. true = commit, using the `expect` token from the prior dry run.

expect.description: The `expect` token returned by the prior dry run — pass it back verbatim. Required to confirm on staging/production profiles.

allowRowDrift.description: Row-count tolerance between the dry run and the confirm. Forced to 0 on production profiles.

tools.name: postgres_update_batch
tools.description: Filtered bulk UPDATE. `where` is a structured, parameterized filter (same shape as postgres_select) and is mandatory — an empty filter is refused before any SQL reaches the server. `set.mode: "uniform"` (the default form) applies one column->value map to every matched row; `set.mode: "perRow"` updates N rows to N different values in one round trip via unnest() joined on a key column. Every identifier is validated against the table's real columns. Two calls. Call it once WITHOUT confirm to get a dry run: the real mutation runs inside a transaction that is always rolled back, and you get back the true row count, up to 20 affected primary keys, and an `expect` token. Read the row count — it is the guard that matters. Then call again with confirm:true and `expect` passed back verbatim; the server recomputes the hash from your arguments (nothing is stored between calls), re-verifies the row count and key checksum INSIDE the committing transaction, and rolls back instead of committing if anything moved. LIMITATION: keyChecksum is md5 over the sorted primary keys of the affected rows, so it detects a different SET of rows (including a substitution that keeps the count identical) but NOT a change to a row's contents when its primary key and the total row count both stayed the same. envClass=production requires `expect` including keyChecksum and forces allowRowDrift to 0 — the one exception is INSERT, which creates the rows it affects instead of selecting pre-existing ones, so there production verifies the row count alone (still with `expect` and the hash). development accepts a bare confirm:true.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

where.description: Filter predicates, ANDed together — required. Empty/omitted is refused before any SQL reaches the server.

values.description: column -> new value, applied to every row `where` matches.

oneOf.description: Default form: the same new values for every matched row.

keyColumn.description: Column identifying each row — typically the primary key. Joined against the rows `where` matches.

rows.description: Update N rows to N different values via unnest() joined on keyColumn.

oneOf.description: Opt-in form: N different rows to N different values in one call.

confirm.description: false/omitted (default) = dry run. true = commit, using the `expect` token from the prior dry run.

expect.description: The `expect` token returned by the prior dry run — pass it back verbatim. Required to confirm on staging/production profiles.

allowRowDrift.description: Row-count tolerance between the dry run and the confirm. Forced to 0 on production profiles.

tools.name: postgres_delete_batch
tools.description: Filtered bulk DELETE. `where` is a structured, parameterized filter (same shape as postgres_select) and is mandatory — an empty filter is refused before any SQL reaches the server; to empty a table deliberately, use postgres_execute_sql with TRUNCATE on a profile that allows DDL. Two calls. Call it once WITHOUT confirm to get a dry run: the real mutation runs inside a transaction that is always rolled back, and you get back the true row count, up to 20 affected primary keys, and an `expect` token. Read the row count — it is the guard that matters. Then call again with confirm:true and `expect` passed back verbatim; the server recomputes the hash from your arguments (nothing is stored between calls), re-verifies the row count and key checksum INSIDE the committing transaction, and rolls back instead of committing if anything moved. LIMITATION: keyChecksum is md5 over the sorted primary keys of the affected rows, so it detects a different SET of rows (including a substitution that keeps the count identical) but NOT a change to a row's contents when its primary key and the total row count both stayed the same. envClass=production requires `expect` including keyChecksum and forces allowRowDrift to 0 — the one exception is INSERT, which creates the rows it affects instead of selecting pre-existing ones, so there production verifies the row count alone (still with `expect` and the hash). development accepts a bare confirm:true.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

where.description: Filter predicates, ANDed together — required. Empty/omitted is refused before any SQL reaches the server.

confirm.description: false/omitted (default) = dry run. true = commit, using the `expect` token from the prior dry run.

expect.description: The `expect` token returned by the prior dry run — pass it back verbatim. Required to confirm on staging/production profiles.

allowRowDrift.description: Row-count tolerance between the dry run and the confirm. Forced to 0 on production profiles.

tools.name: postgres_schema_snapshot
tools.description: Captures a normalized, byte-stable schema snapshot (tables, views, sequences, functions, enums, extensions — see postgres_get_schema for a live equivalent) and writes it to a workspace file as JSON. Use the result with postgres_schema_diff or postgres_prepare_migration to compare it against another snapshot or a live database. Refuses to overwrite an existing file unless overwrite:true.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

schemas.description: Restrict the capture to these schemas. Omit for every schema in scope (Profile.schemas, or every non-system schema).

path.description: Destination file path. Relative paths resolve against the profile's first allowed directory; absolute paths must still land inside an allowed directory.

overwrite.description: Required (true) to replace an existing file at path. Defaults to false.

tools.name: postgres_schema_diff
tools.description: Structural diff between two schema snapshots. Each of before/after is independently either kind:"live" (a fresh capture) or kind:"file" (a file written earlier by postgres_schema_snapshot) — so this compares two files, a file against a live database, or two live databases. Read-only: never modifies either side. An oversized result is truncated with an explicit count and a hint for narrowing scope, never silently cut.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.
Overrides the top-level profile for this side. Defaults to the top-level profile.

schemas.description: Restrict this side's capture to these schemas. Omit for every schema in scope.

path.description: Path to a snapshot file written by postgres_schema_snapshot. Same resolution rules as postgres_export.

profile.description: Profile whose allowed directories this path resolves against. Defaults to the top-level profile.

before.description: The baseline side of the comparison.

profile.description: Overrides the top-level profile for this side. Defaults to the top-level profile.

schemas.description: Restrict this side's capture to these schemas. Omit for every schema in scope.

path.description: Path to a snapshot file written by postgres_schema_snapshot. Same resolution rules as postgres_export.

profile.description: Profile whose allowed directories this path resolves against. Defaults to the top-level profile.

after.description: The changed side of the comparison — the diff reads as "before -> after".

maxChanges.description: Caps the number of changes included before truncation. Defaults to the profile row limit.

tools.name: postgres_prepare_migration
tools.description: Diffs two schema snapshots (same before/after sources as postgres_schema_diff: live database or a file from postgres_schema_snapshot) and returns an ordered, dependency-safe, risk-annotated SQL plan. This tool ONLY emits SQL text — it never runs any of it against any database, under any circumstance. Each statement carries a risk level with a specific reason, an optional precondition query, and either a genuine down statement or an explanation of why one cannot restore the prior state. Change kinds this generator cannot build SQL for are listed in the response's unsupported array, never silently skipped. Review and apply the plan yourself, statement by statement, with postgres_execute_sql or another tool you trust.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.
Overrides the top-level profile for this side. Defaults to the top-level profile.

schemas.description: Restrict this side's capture to these schemas. Omit for every schema in scope.

path.description: Path to a snapshot file written by postgres_schema_snapshot. Same resolution rules as postgres_export.

profile.description: Profile whose allowed directories this path resolves against. Defaults to the top-level profile.

before.description: The baseline side of the comparison.

profile.description: Overrides the top-level profile for this side. Defaults to the top-level profile.

schemas.description: Restrict this side's capture to these schemas. Omit for every schema in scope.

path.description: Path to a snapshot file written by postgres_schema_snapshot. Same resolution rules as postgres_export.

profile.description: Profile whose allowed directories this path resolves against. Defaults to the top-level profile.

after.description: The target side of the comparison — the plan migrates before -> after.

concurrentIndexes.description: Use CREATE/DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY where safe (default true). CONCURRENTLY cannot run in the same transaction block as any other statement in this plan — pass false if you intend to apply the plan as one transaction.

maxStatements.description: Caps the number of statements included before truncation. Defaults to the profile row limit.

tools.name: postgres_admin
tools.description: Widest-blast-radius tool in this server. Six sub-operations selected by `op`: roles_* (create/alter/drop a role), grants_* (GRANT/REVOKE), extensions_* (CREATE/DROP EXTENSION — installing runs arbitrary SQL as superuser), sessions_* (cancel/terminate another backend), maintenance_* (VACUUM/ANALYZE/REINDEX), stats_* (read-only). Every mutating op requires the `admin` capability. `roles_list` (read-only, no capability) lists roles with attributes and memberships. `roles_create`/`roles_alter`/`roles_drop` require the `admin` capability. Password changes are out of scope — use postgres_execute_sql for those. `roles_drop` checks pg_shdepend first and refuses with the exact dependent objects instead of PostgreSQL's raw error when the role still owns something. Two calls. Call it once WITHOUT confirm to get a dry run: the real mutation runs inside a transaction that is always rolled back, and you get back the true row count, up to 20 affected primary keys, and an `expect` token. Read the row count — it is the guard that matters. Then call again with confirm:true and `expect` passed back verbatim; the server recomputes the hash from your arguments (nothing is stored between calls), re-verifies the row count and key checksum INSIDE the committing transaction, and rolls back instead of committing if anything moved. Two calls. Call it once WITHOUT confirm to get a dry run: the real mutation runs inside a transaction that is always rolled back, and you get back the true row count, up to 20 affected primary keys, and an `expect` token. Read the row count — it is the guard that matters. Then call again with confirm:true and `expect` passed back verbatim; the server recomputes the hash from your arguments (nothing is stored between calls), re-verifies the row count and key checksum INSIDE the committing transaction, and rolls back instead of committing if anything moved. WARNING: installing an extension runs that extension's install script as superuser — this can execute arbitrary SQL, not just add functions. Two calls. Call it once WITHOUT confirm to get a dry run: the real mutation runs inside a transaction that is always rolled back, and you get back the true row count, up to 20 affected primary keys, and an `expect` token. tools.name: postgres_backup
tools.description: Runs pg_dump into a file inside the profile's allowed directories. Requires PG_<ALIAS>_ALLOW_BACKUP=true. Scope: the whole database (default), or only the named `schemas` / `tables`. Formats: custom (default, and the one postgres_restore wants), directory, tar, plain (plain is SQL TEXT — pg_restore cannot read it). Writes <path>.partial and renames on success, so a killed pg_dump never leaves a plausible truncated archive, and writes a <path>.meta.json sidecar recording the client major, the server version, the scope and a checksum — postgres_restore reads it to refuse an archive newer than the local pg_restore. There is no dry run: pg_dump is a separate process with no transaction to roll back and nothing to preview. The profile's statement_timeout is NOT applied to the child; use timeoutMs (clamped to PG_<ALIAS>_BACKUP_TIMEOUT_MAX_MS) instead.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

path.description: Destination. Relative paths resolve against the profile's first allowed directory; absolute paths must still land inside one. For format:"directory" this is the directory pg_dump fills.

format.description: custom (default) — compressed, selective restore, the only format postgres_restore prefers. directory — one file per table, restorable in parallel. tar. plain — SQL text, which pg_restore CANNOT read (feed it to psql).

schemas.description: Dump only these schemas (pg_dump --schema). Omit for the whole database.

tables.description: Dump only these tables (pg_dump --table), optionally schema-qualified.

noOwner.description: Omit ownership commands, so the archive restores as whoever runs the restore.

overwrite.description: Required (true) to replace an existing file at path. Defaults to false.

timeoutMs.description: Wall-clock ceiling for the pg_dump child, clamped to PG_<ALIAS>_BACKUP_TIMEOUT_MAX_MS (1 h by default). The profile's statement_timeout is deliberately NOT applied to a backup.

tools.name: postgres_restore
tools.description: THE MOST DESTRUCTIVE TOOL IN THIS SERVER. mode:"restore" runs pg_restore against the profile's database and can overwrite or, with clean:true, DROP AND RECREATE every object in the archive. There is no undo and no rollback: pg_restore is a separate process, so this tool is NOT wrapped in the dry-run/confirm transaction guard the other mutating tools use — there is no transaction this server can roll back, no row count to compare and no expect token to issue. What it has instead: mode:"inspect" (the default) lists the archive contents with pg_restore --list and touches no database, and mode:"restore" refuses without an explicit confirm:true. Requires PG_<ALIAS>_ALLOW_RESTORE=true. The archive must be inside an allowed directory, is size-capped by PG_MCP_MAX_ARCHIVE_BYTES, and is refused when it was written by a NEWER pg_dump than the local pg_restore (archives are forward-only) with the image tag that can read it. Plain-format (SQL text) dumps are not pg_restore archives — feed those to psql.

profile.description: Connection profile alias. Defaults to PG_MCP_DEFAULT_PROFILE.

path.description: Archive written by pg_dump in custom or tar format. Relative paths resolve against the profile's first allowed directory; absolute paths must still land inside one.

mode.description: inspect (default) — list the archive contents, touching no database. restore — apply it. THIS OVERWRITES DATA.

confirm.description: Required (true) for mode:"restore". There is no dry-run/expect token here: pg_restore is a separate process with no transaction this server can roll back. Use mode:"inspect" to see what the archive holds first.

clean.description: pg_restore --clean: DROP every object before recreating it. THE MOST DESTRUCTIVE OPTION IN THIS SERVER — existing data in the target objects is gone.

noOwner.description: Ignore ownership commands in the archive; objects end up owned by the connecting role.

singleTransaction.description: pg_restore --single-transaction: all-or-nothing inside the CHILD process's own transaction. It reduces the blast radius of a partial failure; it is not a dry run and this server cannot roll it back.

schemas.description: Restore only these schemas from the archive (pg_restore --schema).

tables.description: Restore only these tables from the archive (pg_restore --table).

timeoutMs.description: Wall-clock ceiling for the pg_restore child, clamped to PG_<ALIAS>_BACKUP_TIMEOUT_MAX_MS (1 h by default).

instructions: PostgreSQL administration over MCP. Every tool takes an optional `profile` alias; writes, DDL, admin operations and backups are opt-in per profile and refuse by default. Mutating tools are dry-run first: call once to preview, then re-call with `confirm: true` and the returned `expect` object.
